This documentation outlines how to use the BYU supercomputer to run the Point Cloud Maker and Object Detection Learning Software (not yet finished).

See the [Appendix](#appendix) to read about how to execute commands on the supercomputer. 

# Running the pipeline

## 1. Install dependencies and set up your account

While the point cloud code can be run locally, it requires a large amount of processing power. 
To circumvent this, we will use the BYU supercomputer resources. 
The following will walk you through setting up your account and directories. 
Skip to the end of this section to just install the dependencies.

> **Note:** Whenever "username" appears in a file path or terminal input,
> replace it with the username you created when setting up your account.

### Clone this repository

Press the green "Code" button, then copy the URL link it gives. 
Open up your IDE (Integrated Development Environment), like Positron, and download the repository. 
You'll be transferring files to and from this folder, so put it in a good place.

### BYU Supercomputer Account setup

Go to [BYU Research Computing](https://rc.byu.edu/account/create/) and follow the steps for making an account. 
**gmac** is the user that you'll be under, working for Dr. Macfarlane.

Once you've created an account, open the terminal and run the following command
(replace "username" with your username):

```bash
ssh username@ssh.rc.byu.edu
```

> **Note:** You will be required to set up two-factor authentication when you
> first log in. Read about it
> [here](https://rc.byu.edu/wiki/?id=Two-Factor+Authentication). Since BYU uses
> DUO, I find this the easiest to use. But you can use whatever authentication
> app you want.

Every time you log into the terminal, you will be prompted to enter your password and authentication code.
You will then be placed in the `/home/username` directory. 
This is where you will store and run all the files.

### Set up directories

Using the command `mkdir folder_name`, make the following file paths in the
supercomputer terminal in the order given below. This will keep your workspace
organized:

- `/home/username/point_cloud`
- `/home/username/point_cloud/py`
- `/home/username/point_cloud/scjobs`
- `/home/username/point_cloud/data`
- `/home/username/point_cloud/data/log_out`

For example:

```bash
mkdir /home/username/point_cloud
```

### Install a container engine

A major part of the code's backbone is built upon the point cloud densifier code
from [OpenDroneMap](https://github.com/opendronemap/ODM). In order to run the
pipeline, you'll need a container engine:

- **If running locally:** [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) (uses the
  `opendronemap/odm:latest` image, pulled automatically on first run). Not
  suggested due to the amount of computational power needed. 
  If you must use local, talk to Connor first. 

  ```bash
  docker://opendronemap/odm:latest
  ```

- **Using the BYU supercomputer:** [Apptainer](https://apptainer.org/). 
  Apptainer may work locally as well; this has not been verified. 
  Docker for sure does not work on the BYU supercomputer.

  Apptainer isn't on your `PATH` by default — load it first, every time you start
  a new shell session. 
  This command is placed in each .sh job, so it will run automatically each time you submit one.

  ```bash
  module load apptainer
  ```

  Pull the image, then convert it into a sandbox (a plain, uncompressed
  directory). This is required, not optional — some compute nodes on the BYU
  supercomputer can't mount a `.sif` file directly (fails with a
  `squashfuse_ll ... fuse: device not found` error), but a sandbox sidesteps that
  since it doesn't need FUSE to build or to run against.

  In other words, run the following commands on the supercomputer, 
  under the `/home/username/point_cloud/py` directory. 

  ```bash
  apptainer pull odm.sif docker://opendronemap/odm:latest
  apptainer build --sandbox odm_sandbox odm.sif
  ```

### Upload the code and install packages

Upload the `py` and `scjobs` folders to their respective folders in the
supercomputer. Upload `requirements.txt` to `/home/username`.

> **Note:** See the [Appendix](#appendix) at the bottom of this page to see how
> to upload files to the supercomputer.

Once the above is done, run the following command in the supercomputer to install
the required packages:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

You are now ready to run the pipeline using the BYU supercomputer! 🥳

> **Note:** [`py/auto_reconstruct.py`](../py/auto_reconstruct.py) hardcodes the
> path to the sandbox (`APPTAINER_IMAGE`) for the Apptainer/Linux case, since
> that path lives outside this repo and differs per machine/account. 
> It is currently hard coded to `/home/willicon/point_cloud/odm_sandbox`.
> When you download the repository, update that path at the top of the file to point at
> wherever you built `odm_sandbox` above.

## 2. Reconstruction: photos to point cloud

> **Note:** Replace "username" with your username when it shows up in the instructions. 
> See the [Appendix](#appendix) for specific help on how to upload, download, and run files on the supercomputer.

Open the terminal and upload your photos folder to the supercomputer. Input your
username and authentication code and then wait for the files to finish uploading.

In the terminal, run `ssh username@ssh.rc.byu.edu` and enter your password and authentication code. 
Now that you are in the supercomputer terminal, if you have set up the file paths, run:

```bash
nano /home/username/point_cloud/scjobs/auto_reconstruct.sh
```

This will edit the script that runs the code to create the point cloud.

Edit the Python file path under "Run the pipeline" note,
(e.g. `/home/willicon/point_cloud/data/normandy`) so that it reflects the path to your folder with the images. 
Press <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>O</kbd> and <kbd>Enter</kbd> to save the file, 
and <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>X</kbd> to exit.

Change into the folder that will hold all the files showing the terminal output:

```bash
cd /home/username/point_cloud/data/log_out
```

Then submit your job:

```bash
sbatch /home/username/point_cloud/scjobs/auto_reconstruct.sh
```

It will say "Submitted batch job" and then the project number. 
If you want to follow the code output, use `tail -f reconstruct_<jobnumber>.out`. 
Run this in the same location you ran the `sbatch` line.

Once the process is running, you can edit the scjobs file to run another job.

### Configuration

Tuning lives in [`py/config.yml`](../py/config.yml)'s `reconstruction:` section. 
The **same file** is used for both parts of the pipeline. 
Run `nano py/config.yml` before submitting a job to change any of these; 
everything left at `null` is skipped entirely, so OpenSfM's own stock default applies.
See `README.md` or `config.yml` for explanations.

If you want a different config for a specific project instead of editing `py/config.yml` in place, 
save your own copy anywhere and pass `--config /path/to/your.yml` in the .sh file.

### Output

This produces the following inside `data/<project_name>/` itself. 

- `images/`: your source photos, sorted out of any loose files that were sitting
  directly in the project folder
- `reconstruction.json`: camera poses for every registered image; read by
  `building_extractor.py` later for precision-cropping the best photo per building
- `scene_dense.ply`: the point cloud itself, the main deliverable of this stage.
- `config.yaml`: OpenSfM's own per-project config; `auto_reconstruct.py` writes
  `processes` here every run, plus any `reconstruction.*` keys you set to
  something other than `null`, leaving everything else at OpenSfM's stock default

Everything else in the folder (`features/`, `matches/`, `undistorted/` depthmaps
and undistorted images, `tracks.csv`, `camera_models.json`, `*.MRK` files, etc.) is OpenSfM/ODM's own working stuff. 
`building_extractor.py` never reads any of it.

> **Note:** Set `reconstruction.cleanup: true` in `config.yml` to have a
> successful run delete all of that working state automatically, leaving only
> `images/`, `reconstruction.json`, and `scene_dense.ply`. 
> Skipped automatically if `scene_dense.ply` wasn't produced, so a failed run stays debuggable.

## 3. Extraction: point cloud to buildings

> **Note:** Since the process is similar to reconstruction, the following instructions are condensed.

In the supercomputer, change to the log output folder so that the outputs land in
the correct place:

```bash
cd /home/username/point_cloud/data/log_out
```

Edit the extraction job script:

```bash
nano /home/username/point_cloud/scjobs/extract_buildings.sh
```

Edit the Python file path under "Run the pipeline" note,
(e.g. `/home/willicon/point_cloud/data/normandy`) so that it reflects the path to your folder with the images. 
Press <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>O</kbd> and <kbd>Enter</kbd> to save the file, 
and <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>X</kbd> to exit.

Submit your job and wait for it to finish:

```bash
sbatch /home/username/point_cloud/scjobs/extract_buildings.sh
```

The `.out` file is in the form of `house_<jobnumber>.out`.

While it runs, you can edit the `.sh` file to run other jobs.

### Configuration

All settings live in [`py/config.yml`](../py/config.yml).
The **same file** is used for both parts of the pipeline. 
Run `nano py/config.yml` before submitting a job to change any of these; 
everything left at `null` is skipped entirely, so OpenSfM's own stock default applies.
See `README.md` or `config.yml` for explanations.

If you want a different config for a specific project instead of editing `py/config.yml` in place, 
save your own copy anywhere and pass `--config /path/to/your.yml`.

### Output

This produces, in the folder `data/<project_name>/analysis_<project_name>_v9/`, the following:

- `measurements.csv`: one row per building: 
  area (sqft), 
  volume (cuft), 
  height (ft), 
  UTM + lat/lon location, 
  source image references, 
  and two review flags (`Needs_Review` for likely vegetation contamination, `Possible_Vehicle` for
  candidates small/short enough that they might be a parked car rather than a
  building. 
  Source photos come in two views, each with its own three columns
  following the same `{View}_Best_Image` / `{View}_Original_Image` /
  `{View}_Image_Precision_Cropped` pattern:

  - `Nadir_*`: straight-down (DJI gimbal pitch at or steeper than
    `imagery.nadir_pitch_threshold` in `config.yml`, default -65.0°)

  - `Oblique_*`: the shallower of the site's two survey passes, if it has one —
    not a true side-on elevation shot, but steep enough to still show real
    wall/facade detail a nadir shot can't.

    > **Warning:** The default -65° threshold is not universal.
    > Check the "Indexed N nadir + M oblique" line in a run's log against what you
    > actually expect before trusting either view on a new site, and adjust
    > `imagery.nadir_pitch_threshold` in the config if it looks wrong.

    `{View}_Image_Precision_Cropped` says whether that view's `Best_Image` / `Original_Image` is a verified precision crop (projected from the building's real 3D footprint into a registered photo) or just the closest-by-GPS fallback photo, uncropped and unverified. 
    Only trust the image as accurate when this is `True`. 
    Oblique has no fallback at all: if precision cropping fails for that view, `Oblique_Best_Image` is `N/A` and there's no oblique photo for that building.

- `individual_houses/`: per-building `.ply` point clouds

- `best_images/` and `best_images_cropped/` — source photos and crops for each
  building, one pair per view (`{house_ID}_nadir.jpg` / `{house_ID}_oblique.jpg`).
  A cropped file only exists when that view's `Image_Precision_Cropped` is `True`

# Appendix {#appendix}

## Uploading to and downloading from the supercomputer

To upload a folder/file to the supercomputer, you'll run a command composed of
the following pieces:

```bash
scp -r /path/from/local/computer username@ssh.rc.byu.edu:/home/path/to/output/location
```

- `scp -r` tells the terminal you want to access a remote network, and that you
  want to transfer a folder/file to or from that network.
- `/path/from/local/computer`, the first path, is the file/folder that you want to send. 
  The path `/Users/connor/Desktop/normandy` will send the `normandy` folder from my local desktop.
- `username@ssh.rc.byu.edu:/home/username/point_cloud/data`, the second path, is
  the location where you want to send the file. 
  This path `username@ssh.rc.byu.edu:/home/username/point_cloud/data` will send the 
  file/folder to the BYU supercomputer in the `point_cloud/data` folder.

> **Note:** When uploading, always place the local path first, then the supercomputer path. 
> **Linux, what the BYU computer runs, is case sensitive.** 
> So keep that in mind.

To download a folder/file from the supercomputer, switch the second and third
argument. Place the supercomputer path first, then the local path, like this:

```bash
scp -r willicon@ssh.rc.byu.edu:/home/willicon/point_cloud/data /Users/willicon/Desktop/normandy/scene_dense.ply
```

Whenever you upload or download, you will have to input your password and
authentication code. It's annoying, but there is no way around it.

## Creating and running jobs on the BYU supercomputer

The BYU supercomputer uses `Slurm` commands to run its jobs. 
Their [documentation](https://rc.byu.edu/wiki/?id=Slurm) and
[videos](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i1r9BxHBG0I&list=PL326A5EB4E3B16FED) are
old and somewhat outdated, but worth a look through. 
Below is the minimum you need to run the pipeline.

### nano

This command lets you edit files that are on the supercomputer. 
Type `nano` and then the file path to the file you want to edit. 
Remember, Linux is case sensitive.

```bash
nano /home/username/point_cloud/scjobs/auto_reconstruct.sh
```
Press <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>O</kbd> and <kbd>Enter</kbd> to save the file, 
and <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>X</kbd> to exit.

### sbatch

This command runs the job commands on the supercomputer.
Like `nano`, type `sbatch` and then the path to the `.sh` file you want to run. 
Don't try to run `.py` files, it won't work. 

```bash
sbatch /home/username/point_cloud/scjobs/auto_reconstruct.sh
```

## Useful supercomputer commands

| Task | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Change file directory | `cd path/to/folder` | |
| See all files/folders in the current directory | `ls` | |
| Move a file | `mv /path/to/current/location /path/to/new/destination/` | |
| Submit your job | `sbatch [name of .sh file where job script is saved]` | |
| Edit a file | `nano path/to/file` | <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>O</kbd> to save, <kbd>Control</kbd> + <kbd>X</kbd> to exit |
| Check on the status of a job | `scontrol show job [job number]` | |
| Check the status of all jobs | `squeue -u username` | |
| Cancel jobs | `scancel [job ID(s)]` | |
| Follow output for code | `tail -f (reconstruct or house)_(job number).out` | e.g. `tail -f reconstruct_1234567.out` |
| Remove files | `rm filename1 filename2 etc` | |
| Remove folders | `rm -r foldername` | |
